Electrical discharge machining is frequently adopted for difficult-to-machine nickel‑chromium alloys such as Hastelloy C‑22 because conventional machining is often ineffective for these materials. (Nowicki et al. 2022) The physical and mechanical properties of the tool electrode directly influence process efficiency, machining accuracy, and surface roughness in EDM of such alloys. (Nowicki et al. 2022) Recent studies report a marked trend toward using graphite electrodes, motivated by low raw-material cost, good machinability, and high sublimation temperature. (Nowicki et al. 2022)

Two recent experimental investigations specifically evaluated POCO graphite electrodes with fine (≈1 µm) and coarser (≈10 µm) grain sizes when machining Hastelloy C‑22. (Nowicki et al. 2022) Those studies found that finer-grained graphite increases process efficiency and reduces tool wear, while coarser-grained graphite yields higher material removal rates but also higher relative tool wear; fine grains produced lower surface roughness (Ra). (Nowicki et al. 2024) (Nowicki et al. 2022) The mechanism proposed links detached graphite grains to discharge stability: grain detachment affects spark stability and thus process efficiency. (Nowicki et al. 2024)

Across the cited experiments, electrical parameters emerge repeatedly as the dominant drivers of MRR, TWR and Ra. (Nowicki et al. 2022) Both discharge current (peak current) and pulse duration (pulse‑on time) are reported as the main factors controlling MRR and Ra for the graphite electrodes studied. (Nowicki et al. 2022) One factorial/Taguchi study on a corrosion‑resistant superalloy (with cryogenic treatments) likewise identified peak current and pulse‑on time among the most influential parameters, with ANOVA attributing the largest shares of variance in MRR and Ra to peak current. (Nas & Kara 2022) A Taguchi/ANOVA study on titanium also found amperage to be the most effective factor for MRR and TWR. (Akıncıoğlu 2022) For electrode geometry and wear phenomena during machining of Hastelloy B2, current and pulse duration strongly affect electrode taper, radius, and wear length, with unstable sparks producing rounding of sharp edges. (Ramabalan et al. 2024)

Several works survey and test auxiliary methods to mitigate high tool wear, low MRR, and poor surface integrity in EDM. (Shastri et al. 2022) Approaches include cryogenic treatment, powder‑mixed dielectrics, ultrasonic assistance, and process variants; modelling and optimisation studies (ANN, MOGA, Taguchi) have been used to predict and reduce electrode wear and overcut in other material systems. (Shastri et al. 2022) (Sana et al. 2024) Electrical discharge coating (EDC) is discussed as a related surface‑modification technology, summarising process parameters and coating characteristics, though not specifically applied to Hastelloy electrodes in the provided sources. (Liew et al. 2020)

The evidence on graphite electrodes shows grain size influences both process efficiency and surface finish in EDM of Hastelloy C-22. Experimental comparisons using POCO graphite with 1 µm and 10 µm grain sizes report that larger-grained graphite yields higher material removal rates but also higher relative tool wear, while finer-grained graphite produces lower surface roughness. (Nowicki et al. 2022) Graphite with miniaturized grain size is reported to increase process efficiency and reduce tool wear, and detached graphite grains are said to affect discharge stability and process effectiveness; these observations were used to develop predictive mathematical models for MRR, relative TWR and Ra under negative polarity EDM of Hastelloy C‑22. (Nowicki et al. 2024)

Across studies of nickel‑based and other difficult‑to‑machine alloys, discharge current (peak current) and pulse duration (pulse‑on time) consistently emerge as the principal process parameters driving MRR and surface roughness. (Nowicki et al. 2022) (Nowicki et al. 2024) One factorial/Taguchi investigation found peak current to be the dominant factor controlling both MRR and Ra—accounting for the largest percentage of explained variance in that experiment—while optimal combinations included lower pulse‑on times for improved Ra and MRR in cryogenically treated samples. (Nas & Kara 2022) ANOVA and regression analyses in EDM studies of other alloys likewise identify amperage as the most influential factor for MRR and TWR. (Akıncıoğlu 2022)

Evidence on electrode wear behaviour and dimensional effects highlights that current and pulse duration strongly affect electrode geometry and wear morphology. (Ramabalan et al. 2024) Thermal diffusion from unstable sparks can transform sharp electrode edges into hemispherical ends, increasing electrode wear length and altering taper and radius. (Ramabalan et al. 2024) Reviews of EDM adaptations enumerate multiple strategies—cryogenic treatment, powder‑mixed dielectric, ultrasonic assistance and others—aimed at reducing TWR, increasing MRR, or improving surface integrity, indicating an active area of experimental mitigation approaches. (Shastri et al. 2022) (Sana et al. 2024)

The reviewed material discusses electrical discharge coating technologies and surface modification by EDM processes but does not provide data on copper electrodes or on composite electrodes used specifically against Hastelloy in terms of TWR, MRR, or parameter sensitivity. Electrical discharge machining of Hastelloy alloys shows strong sensitivity to the electrode material and the machining parameters, with multiple studies linking electrode physical properties and process settings to material removal rate (MRR), tool wear rate (TWR), and surface roughness (Ra). Experimental work on Hastelloy C-22 using POCO graphite electrodes with different grain sizes found that larger-grained graphite increases process efficiency (higher MRR) but also increases relative tool wear, while finer-grained graphite produced lower surface roughness. (Nowicki et al. 2022) The same trend is reiterated in a later study that introduced fine-grained (1 µm) and coarser (10 µm) POCO graphite electrodes and concluded that fine-grained graphite increases process efficiency and reduces tool wear, with detached graphite grains affecting discharge stability and process effectiveness. (Nowicki et al. 2024)

Discharge current and pulse duration (pulse-on time) repeatedly emerge as the dominant electrical parameters controlling MRR, TWR and Ra in the cited experiments. Nowicki et al. identified discharge current and pulse duration as the main factors determining MRR and Ra for both fine- and coarse-grained graphite, and found the time interval (pulse-off) to be dominant for relative graphite wear. (Nowicki et al. 2022) Other parametric studies on superalloys and difficult-to-machine materials likewise report peak current (amperage) and pulse-on time as the most influential factors: one Taguchi–ANOVA study found peak current to explain the largest shares of variance for MRR and Ra, and another EDM investigation reported amperage as the most effective factor across MRR, TWR and surface metrics. (Nas & Kara 2022) (Akıncıoğlu 2022) Ramabalan et al. observed that current and pulse duration greatly affect electrode wear and edge transformation, noting that unstable sparks and heat diffusion reshape sharp electrode features during EDM of Hastelloy B2. Several mitigation and enhancement strategies reported in the literature alter electrode behaviour or the machining environment to improve TWR and dimensional accuracy. Reviews and experimental studies discuss combining EDM with cryogenic treatments, powder-mixed dielectrics, ultrasonic assistance, and coating techniques to modify surface integrity and performance metrics; these works frame such combinations as responses to the persistent challenges of high TWR, low MRR and poor surface quality. (Shastri et al. 2022) (Liew et al. 2020) Studies on electrode treatment and dielectric modification (for other alloys) report substantial reductions in electrode wear and dimensional inaccuracy when using treated electrodes or nanopowder-mixed dielectrics, indicating potential routes to improve EDM outcomes. Multiple sources identify discharge current (peak current or amperage) and pulse duration (pulse‑on time) as primary drivers of MRR and surface roughness in EDM. Experimental designs applying factorial, Taguchi and ANOVA analyses conclude that peak current most strongly affects MRR and Ra, and that pulse duration is likewise influential; one Taguchi analysis quantified peak current as accounting for the majority of variance in MRR and Ra for treated and untreated specimens in a cryogenic‑treatment study. Work addressing electrode shape change and wear mechanisms shows that high currents and long pulse durations promote extensive electrode degradation and geometric transformation. Square electrodes used to produce square holes in Hastelloy B2 rapidly blunt and evolve into hemispherical ends due to unstable sparking and heat diffusion, with current and pulse duration greatly affecting electrode taper, radius and wear length. (Ramabalan et al. 2024) Broader reviews of EDM emphasise persistent challenges of high TWR, low MRR and poor surface integrity caused by continuous sparking, and they summarise a range of mitigation strategies including cryogenic treatment, powder‑mixed EDM and ultrasonic assistance. (Shastri et al. 2022) (Sana et al. 2024)

Fine‑grained graphite studies propose mathematical models for parameter selection to balance efficiency, wear and roughness, while nanopowder and cryogenic electrode treatments have been modelled with ANNs and optimisation algorithms to reduce electrode wear and overcut in other materials. (Nowicki et al. 2024) (Sana et al. 2024) However, these investigations focus on specific electrode types (graphite grades) or on electrode treatments in different material contexts rather than directly comparing conventional (e.g., copper or brass) and composite electrodes on Hastelloy. Selective Laser Melting (SLM) produces near-full-density metallic parts by layer-wise melting and fusion of powder with a high-power laser, enabling near net-shape components with up to 99.9% relative density. (Yap et al. 2015) Metal AM, and SLM in particular, imparts unique microstructural features in steels—hierarchical subgrains and fine precipitates—that can enhance strength, wear and corrosion resistance compared with conventional routes, while also acting as an intrinsic heat treatment that induces in situ phase transformations and tempering phenomena. (Haghdadi et al. 2020)

As-built SLM maraging steel commonly shows a very fine martensitic microstructure produced by extremely high cooling rates. Tan et al. observed submicron grain sizes (0.31 μm on average) indicating cooling rates up to 10^7 K/s and reported a martensitic matrix containing dense needle-shaped Ni3X (X = Ti, Al, Mo) nanoprecipitates that account for age hardening. (Tan et al. 2018) Ahmadkhaniha et al. similarly found a fine-grained martensitic structure in as-printed maraging steel, with isotropic microstructure across build sections and a relatively high surface roughness (Ra ≈ 10 μm). (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) These as-built features combine high strength with residual stresses and surface roughness that influence subsequent properties. (Tan et al. 2018)(Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

Post-build heat treatments substantially modify the microstructure and properties. Systematic heat-treatment studies detected phase-transformation temperatures and applied aging to develop precipitation strengthening and to relieve residual stress, with heat treatments producing the maximum nano-hardness associated with precipitation and also affecting corrosion potentials. (Tan et al. 2018)(Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) Godec et al. investigated combinations of solution treatment, aging and plasma nitriding, showing that prior heat treatment influences the morphology and chemistry of thermochemical layers and that nitriding performed without prior aging led to cracking in the compound layer. (Godec et al. 2021) These reports indicate that heat-treatment history dictates precipitate state, residual stress relief and compatibility with follow-up surface treatments. (Tan et al. 2018)(Godec et al. 2021)

Austenite reversion (reversed austenite) after intercritical or tempering treatments has been identified in SLM maraging steels and linked to both mechanical and corrosion behaviour. Khan et al. tempered specimens near austenite-forming temperatures and found reversed austenite nucleating mainly along martensite lath boundaries, promoted by local Ni enrichment from intermetallic dissolution. (Khan et al. 2022) They report that this reversed austenite correlates with improved pitting resistance compared to as-printed, aged, or homogenized specimens. (Khan et al. 2022)

Corrosion studies in chloride environments indicate that microstructure and surface condition strongly control performance. Khan et al. performed electrochemical tests in 3.5 wt% NaCl and found that the 720 °C intercritical-tempered specimen exhibited higher pitting potential and lower corrosion current density and rate than other conditions, concluding that reversed austenite enhances pitting resistance. (Khan et al. 2022) Ahmadkhaniha et al. compared corrosion behaviour of as-printed and heat-treated SLM maraging steel with wrought counterparts and found that despite finer microstructure the corrosion behaviour in heat-treated conditions was similar, with precipitation playing a primary role in both hardness and corrosion response; they also showed electropolishing markedly reduced surface roughness. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) Godec et al. linked prior heat treatment to improved corrosion resistance after plasma nitriding, while nitriding without prior aging produced defects that impair performance. (Godec et al. 2021)
rows.b:
SLM intrinsically yields near-full density parts by layerwise melting and solidification, a process associated with extremely high cooling rates that produce submicron grain sizes and in situ precipitation in powder‑bed fused maraging steels (Yap et al. 2015)(Tan et al. 2018).

Electron microscopy in optimised SLM 300‑grade maraging steel revealed an average submicron grain size (~0.31 μm) and dense arrays of needle‑shaped Ni3X precipitates that account for age hardening, while heat treatments both strengthen and relieve residual stress and reduce anisotropy to some extent (Tan et al. 2018)(Haghdadi et al. 2020).

Heat treatment and thermochemical processing modify the SLM microstructure and thereby affect corrosion and wear performance. Studies that combined solution treatment, aging and plasma nitriding found that prior heat treatment influenced the morphology and integrity of nitrided layers on SLM 18Ni‑300: nitriding without prior aging produced cracks in the compound layer, whereas nitriding of prior‑heat‑treated SLM material improved wear and corrosion resistance relative to untreated SLM samples (Godec et al. 2021). Likewise, conventional heat treatments such as aging change precipitation states and corrosion potentials: aging produced maximum nano‑hardness and more negative corrosion potentials in a comparison of SLM and wrought maraging steel, with precipitation identified as the primary factor governing both hardness and corrosion behaviour (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021).

Reversion to austenite during intercritical heat treatment (austenite reversion) is reported to alter pitting resistance in chloride environments. Tempering within the α’ + γ domain produced reversed austenite along martensite lath boundaries, associated with local nickel enrichment from intermetallic dissolution; specimens tempered at 720 °C showed higher pitting potential, lower corrosion current density and lower corrosion rate in 3.5 wt% NaCl than as‑printed, aged, or homogenised specimens, indicating that reversed austenite can enhance pitting resistance in chloride solutions (Khan et al. 2022).

Despite these findings, gaps remain regarding how SLM‑specific microstructural heterogeneities (layerwise effects, residual stress, surface roughness) interact quantitatively with heat‑treatment‑induced phases (precipitates, reversed austenite) to control corrosion in chloride environments, and how thermochemical routes like simultaneous nitriding/aging can be optimally applied without inducing nitride layer defects (Tan et al. 2018)(Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)(Godec et al. 2021). Selective Laser Melting (SLM) produces near fully dense maraging-steel parts by layerwise laser melting and rapid solidification, a process known to impart unique microstructural features such as very fine prior-β and martensitic substructures due to extremely high cooling rates. (Yap et al. 2015) These process-induced features act as an intrinsic heat treatment in some AM steels, promoting hierarchical (sub)grains and fine precipitates that modify mechanical and corrosion-related properties relative to conventionally produced counterparts. (Haghdadi et al. 2020)

Studies of as-built SLM 18Ni-300 (grade 300) maraging steel consistently report a fine martensitic matrix with very small grain/subgrain sizes and in-situ precipitation. Tan et al. detected submicron grain sizes (~0.31 μm average) and dense, needle-shaped Ni3X precipitates in the as-fabricated martensitic matrix, attributing these features to cooling rates on the order of 10^7 K/s and linking the precipitates to subsequent age hardening. (Tan et al. 2018) Ahmadkhaniha et al. likewise report a fine-grained martensitic structure in the as-printed condition and note the absence of strong texture or anisotropy across build directions. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

Heat treatments alter this baseline microstructure through precipitation, residual-stress relief, and possible phase reversion. Tan et al. show that deliberate heat treatments induce strengthened precipitate distributions, reduce residual stresses, and somewhat reduce mechanical anisotropy compared with the as-fabricated state. (Tan et al. 2018) Godec et al. explored combinations of solution treatment, aging and plasma nitriding, finding that prior heat treatment affects the morphology and chemistry of subsequent nitride layers and the associated wear and corrosion response. (Godec et al. 2021) Ahmadkhaniha et al. compared SLM and wrought maraging steel after heat treatments and reported similar nano-hardness and corrosion behaviour in heat-treated conditions, with aging producing maximum nano-hardness and the lowest corrosion potentials; they identify precipitation as the dominant factor governing both hardness and corrosion response. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

Austenite reversion during intercritical tempering has been investigated for its mechanical and corrosion effects. Khan et al. tempered SLM maraging steel near austenite-forming temperatures and observed reversed austenite precipitated mainly along martensite lath boundaries; they attribute nucleation to local Ni enrichment from intermetallic dissolution. (Khan et al. 2022) Importantly, that study directly links reversed austenite to improved pitting resistance: the specimen tempered at 720 °C showed higher pitting potential, lower corrosion current density, and lower corrosion rate in 3.5 wt% NaCl than as-printed, aged, and homogenized samples without reversed austenite. (Khan et al. 2022)

Reviews of AM steels emphasise both potential corrosion benefits and remaining gaps. Haghdadi et al. summarise that AM-induced fine grains and precipitates can enhance corrosion resistance relative to conventional steels but note challenges remain in achieving acceptable ductility and fatigue behavior. (Haghdadi et al. 2020) Afkhami et al. highlight that many process and post-process variables (orientation, heat treatment, surface quality) influence performance and identify gaps in understanding that also affect corrosion-relevant properties. Selective Laser Melting (SLM) builds parts by melting and fusing metallic powders layer by layer using a high-power laser, producing near-full-density components suitable for functional testing and property studies. (Yap et al. 2015)

Evidence shows as-built SLM maraging steel exhibits a very fine martensitic microstructure with nanoscale precipitates formed in situ by the rapid thermal cycles of the process. (Tan et al. 2018) Electron microscopy in one study revealed submicron grains (0.31 μm average) and abundant needle-shaped Ni3X (X = Ti, Al, Mo) nanoprecipitates within a martensitic matrix, which account for age hardening in the as-fabricated state. (Tan et al. 2018) A complementary microstructural survey found a fine-grained martensitic structure with no preferred texture and similar morphology across build sections in as-printed SLM maraging steel. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) Layerwise thermal histories in SLM act as intrinsic heat treatments, producing hierarchical subgrains and fine precipitates that distinguish AM microstructures from conventionally processed steels. (Haghdadi et al. 2020)

Studies that compare heat-treated conditions report that deliberate post-build aging, solution treatment and intercritical tempering modify precipitate populations, residual stress, and phase fractions. (Tan et al. 2018) One investigation tempered specimens near the austenite-forming range (intercritical treatment at 720°C) and found reversed austenite precipitated mainly along martensite lath boundaries, nucleated where local Ni enrichment followed dissolution of intermetallics. (Khan et al. 2022) Another work explored the interaction of solution treatment, aging and subsequent plasma nitriding on SLM 18Ni-300, reporting that prior heat treatment influenced the morphology and integrity of nitrided layers and that nitriding without prior aging led to cracks in the compound layer. (Godec et al. 2021)

Corrosion performance in chloride media appears sensitive to these microstructural changes and surface condition. (Haghdadi et al. 2020) One experimental study measured pitting behaviour in 3.5 wt% NaCl and reported that the 720°C-tempered specimen with reversed austenite exhibited a higher pitting potential, lower corrosion current density, and lower corrosion rate than as-printed, aged, or homogenized specimens without reversed austenite. (Khan et al. 2022) Comparative testing of SLM and wrought maraging steel after heat treatment found similar nano-hardness and corrosion behaviour, with precipitation state controlling both hardness and corrosion potential; electropolishing substantially reduced SLM surface roughness and was assessed for its effect on corrosion. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) The combined study of nitriding and heat treatment concluded that thermochemical treatment following appropriate prior heat treatments can improve wear and corrosion resistance, whereas inappropriate sequences caused defects in the nitride layer. (Godec et al. 2021)

Despite these findings, the literature leaves unresolved how specific SLM thermal histories, resulting phase fractions (including reversed austenite), and surface condition quantitatively interact to determine chloride-induced pitting across process parameter ranges and post-treatments. (Khan et al. 2022)(Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)(Tan et al. 2018)(Godec et al. 2021)

Parasad et al. find that government subsidies act as a primary motivator by helping to overcome the initial investment risk in rooftop PV adoption, and that low prices and low maintenance costs further mitigate long-term apprehension about returns and upkeep. (Parsad et al. 2020) Aarakit et al. report that affordability is the main driver of which type of solar PV system households adopt in Uganda, and that flexible payment mechanisms increase uptake among income-constrained households. (Aarakit et al. 2021) Tanveer et al. likewise show perceived cost has a negative effect on consumers' willingness to adopt household solar PV in Pakistan. (Tanveer et al. 2021)

Related to cost, policy instruments and subsidies matter both as direct financial support and as part of broader institutional enabling environments. India’s national targets for solar capacity reflect an explicit policy push toward rooftop deployment, with a stated goal for 40 GW of grid-connected rooftop PV within the country’s larger solar targets. (Goel 2016) Reviews of India’s renewable energy policy landscape characterize strong government support and a range of programs intended to attract investment and scale deployment, while also noting persistent obstacles in the sector. Randomized and experimental studies of diabetes self-management apps report inconsistent effects on glycaemic control. A multicentre pragmatic randomized controlled trial of the FDA-cleared BlueStar app found no difference in mean HbA1c between intervention and control arms at 3 months. (Agarwal et al. 2018) An exploratory, within-intervention analysis of the same trial found an association between greater app use and small reductions in HbA1c, estimating a 0.016-point decrease in 3-month HbA1c for each additional day of app use. (Agarwal et al. 2018) Smaller pilot work in other diabetes populations has increased self-monitoring behaviors but did not demonstrate HbA1c improvements within the pilot timeframe and sample size, noting that demonstrating HbA1c change will require adequately powered, longer trials. (Cafazzo et al. 2012) Systematic syntheses across health-related app interventions similarly report a mixed picture: many studies show behavior change in the direction intended, yet the included trials vary in quality and most authors call for larger, high-quality randomized trials to establish clinical outcomes. (Zhao et al. 2016)

Engagement with diabetes apps is variable and context-dependent. Trial data show low and heterogeneous usage: in the BlueStar trial overall app use was low and median days of use differed markedly by clinical site, indicating strong contextual effects on engagement. (Agarwal et al. 2018) Reviews of app interventions across behaviors report retention in intervention groups typically at or above 60% in the short term, but these studies were assessed as having some risk of bias and varied follow-up durations. (Zhao et al. 2016) Pilot and qualitative studies document increases in specific self-management actions (for example, blood glucose checks) when apps include automated data capture and immediate prompts, but these usage gains were measured over weeks rather than months. (Cafazzo et al. 2012)

Across qualitative, usability and content-evaluation studies, features linked to uptake and sustained use cluster around usability, relevance, and perceived usefulness. Systematic coding of user perspectives identified barriers and facilitators mapping to themes such as perceived motivators, information and personalised guidance, tracking for awareness, credibility, goal setting, reminders, and concerns about sharing personal information. (Peng et al. 2016) Empirical syntheses highlight design elements that improve effectiveness and likely support continued use: low time burden, user-friendly interfaces, real-time feedback, individualized content, detailed information, and health professional involvement. (Zhao et al. 2016) Studies of commercial diabetes apps show many prioritize reporting and reminders over personalised education or therapeutic support, indicating a mismatch between common app features and user-desired functions linked to sustained engagement. (Izahar et al. 2017) Concerns about app quality, privacy, device connectivity and the need for regulatory or certification approaches are recurrent, suggesting that perceived credibility and safety also influence whether users continue engaging with an app. (Boulos et al. 2014)

Taken together, the evidence shows that app-driven behavior change and downstream HbA1c effects depend on both the presence of engagement-promoting features and the context in which apps are implemented; however, heterogeneous study designs, short follow-up, and variable usage limit causal attribution of glycaemic outcomes to apps themselves. (Zhao et al. 2016)(Agarwal et al. 2018)

(Agarwal et al. 2018) A pilot study in adolescents using a gamified app increased frequency of glucose monitoring but noted that demonstrating improvements in HbA1c would require a larger, longer study and linking incentives to decision-making based on readings. Qualitative and app-content studies identify specific design and contextual features associated with adoption and sustained use. (Huis et al. 2017)

rows.a:
Entrepreneurship supported by microfinance is associated with measurable gains in several dimensions of women’s empowerment, but these gains are uneven across domains. A quasi-experimental mixed-methods study found that female entrepreneurs outperform non-entrepreneurs on economic, psychological and overall empowerment indicators, while impacts on political and social empowerment are smaller or mixed; qualitative interviews in the same study corroborated that entrepreneurship can serve as an effective tool for holistic empowerment, conditional on women exerting full control over their ventures. (Khan et al. 2022)

However, the pathway from credit to sustained business growth and profit is shaped by factors beyond access to loans. A seven‑year quasi-experiment that combined an ICT intervention with an examination of women’s social networks in rural India found large differences in business formation attributable to ICT: 160 new businesses opened in intervention villages versus 40 in controls, and network position and ties to family or to men in power altered both the initiation and profitability of ventures. (Venkatesh et al. 2017) This evidence implies that information access and social connectivity amplify the returns to entrepreneurship in ways that credit alone does not address. (Venkatesh et al. 2017)

Multiple reviews and theoretical treatments emphasize that institutional form, program design, and social context mediate microfinance impacts. A comprehensive review of microfinance literature highlights open questions about sustainability, targeting, products and impact assessment that bear on whether credit programs translate into entrepreneurial development for women. (Brau & Woller 2004) At the industry level, analyses of microfinance institutions stress that commercialization and profit motives change which customers are served, suggesting that market-driven scaling may leave gaps in reaching the poorest women best served by mission-driven providers. (Cull et al. 2009)

Critically, credit can also produce adverse outcomes when social and market dynamics are not considered. Ethnographic work in Bangladesh documented rising indebtedness and worsening vulnerabilities in some communities, and argued that market-based interventions like microfinance can undermine social capital that otherwise supports entrepreneurial capability. (Banerjee & Jackson 2016) Complementary qualitative studies show that women’s enterprises that embed innovations within local social and cultural norms—what the authors call emancipatory social entrepreneurship—can both empower women and contribute to changing restrictive social orders. (Haugh & Talwar 2014)

Conceptual syntheses recommend distinguishing dimensions and timing of empowerment to interpret heterogeneous findings: a Three‑Dimensional Model separates personal, relational, and societal empowerment, and highlights that time lags and cultural context influence which dimensions emerge after an intervention. (Huis et al. 2017) [[NEEDS SOURCE: household decision-making effects and intra-household outcomes]]
rows.b:
The evidence on whether microfinance expands women’s businesses shows heterogeneous effects driven by complementary inputs such as information technology and social networks. A seven-year quasi-experiment in 20 rural Indian villages found a large ICT-driven increase in new businesses—160 in treated villages versus 40 in controls—while also showing that ties to family and community amplify both entrepreneurial activity and profit when combined with ICT use; ties to men in power had negative associations with ICT uptake and entrepreneurship unless those ties were weak. (Venkatesh et al. 2017) Khan et al.’s mixed-method study found that female entrepreneurs supported by microfinance are better off on economic indicators than non-entrepreneurs, based on quantitative comparisons of 132 entrepreneurs and 238 non-entrepreneurs and corroborating qualitative interviews. (Khan et al. 2022) Taken together, these studies indicate that credit alone may produce limited business growth unless paired with other resources or enabling conditions such as ICT and supportive social ties. (Venkatesh et al. 2017)(Khan et al. 2022)

The literature on empowerment demonstrates that effects are multi-dimensional and temporally and culturally contingent. A synthesis proposes a Three-Dimensional Model—micro (personal), meso (relational), and macro (societal)—and argues that time lags and cultural context shape when and which dimensions change after microfinance interventions. (Huis et al. 2017) Empirical work supports partial empowerment: Khan et al. report improvements across economic, psychological and some social dimensions for entrepreneurs, but note relatively smaller gains in political and social empowerment and that non-entrepreneurs also show social empowerment in the same setting. (Khan et al. 2022)(Huis et al. 2017) Thus, studies converge on the claim that empowerment is neither unidimensional nor immediate, and measurement must distinguish personal, relational and societal outcomes. (Huis et al. 2017)(Khan et al. 2022)

Evidence also highlights limits and potential harms of market-based microfinance when credit is not embedded in social or regulatory safeguards. An ethnographic study of three Bangladeshi villages found that microfinance increased indebtedness and exacerbated economic, social and environmental vulnerabilities, and that social capital can be undermined by market-based interventions. (Banerjee & Jackson 2016) Analysis of the microfinance industry stresses that commercialization and profit motives shape who is served and that subsidies and mission-oriented institutions play a role in reaching poorer clients; the market alone cannot fill all gaps. (Cull et al. 2009) These findings suggest that without attention to mission, regulation and complementary supports, credit can produce adverse outcomes or fail to reach those who need it most. (Banerjee & Jackson 2016)(Cull et al. 2009)

Social entrepreneurship and culturally attuned business processes can enable women’s economic activity while conforming to local norms and, in some cases, shift the social order. Qualitative work in North India shows that innovative processes which both facilitate economic activity and comply with social norms contributed to changing the social order and framed emancipatory social entrepreneurship as simultaneously empowering and socially transformative. (Haugh & Talwar 2014)

What remains unresolved is how specific combinations of credit, ICT, social networks, and program design produce sustained business growth and movement across the three empowerment dimensions in different cultural settings; empirical comparisons that isolate these complementarities over time are scarce. (Venkatesh et al. 2017)(Huis et al. 2017)(Khan et al. 2022)
